etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English basket, from Anglo-Norman bascat, of obscure origin.

One theory is that it derives from Late Latin bascauda (“kettle, table-vessel”), from Proto-Brythonic (in Breton baskodenn), from Proto-Celtic *baskis (“bundle, load”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰask- (“bundle”). Related to Latin fascis (“bundle, package, load”). Doublet of fasces.

definitions.definition: (by extension) A bed for a cat.
A lightweight container, generally round, open at the top, and tapering toward the bottom.
A wire or plastic container similar in shape to a basket, used for carrying articles for purchase in a shop.
(Internet) In an online shop, a listing of a customer's chosen items before they are ordered.
(figurative) A set or collection of intangible things.

quote.citation: 2004, Gichinga Ndirangu, Heinrich Böll Foundation (Nairobi, Kenya), An African civil society action toward WTO 2003 (page 16)
quote.text: The basket of issues that developing countries had vigorously wanted addressed such as agriculture, SANDD and implementation-related issues were given scant attention by developed countries for most part of the conference.

definitions.definition: (basketball) A circular hoop, from which a net is suspended, which is the goal through which the players try to throw the ball.
(basketball) The act of putting the ball through the basket, thereby scoring points.
(uncountable) The game of basketball.

A dance movement in some line dances, where men put their arms round the women's lower backs, and the women put their arms over the men's shoulders, and the group (usually of four, any more is difficult) spins round, which should result in the women's feet leaving the ground.
(LGBTQ, slang) The penis and region surrounding it.[1]
(slang) The bulge of the penis seen through clothing.
(obsolete) In a stage-coach, two outside seats facing each other.

quote.citation: 1773, Oliver Goldsmith, She Stoops to Conquer:
quote.text: In my time, the follies of the town crept slowly among us, but now they travel faster than a stage-coach. Its fopperies come down not only as inside passengers, but in the very basket.

definitions.definition: A singlestick with a basket hilt.

quote.citation: 1773, Oliver Goldsmith, She Stoops to Conquer:
quote.text: Baw! damme, but I'll fight you both, one after the other——with baskets.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A protection for the hand on a sword or a singlestick; a guard of a bladed weapon.
(ballooning) The gondola or wicker basket suspended from the balloon, in which the pilot and passengers travel.

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, David Simpson, “Fantasy of navigation”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 36:
quote.text: Like most human activities, ballooning has sponsored heroes and hucksters and a good deal in between. For every dedicated scientist patiently recording atmospheric pressure and wind speed while shivering at high altitudes, there is a carnival barker with a bevy of pretty girls willing to dangle from a basket or parachute down to earth.

definitions.definition: (architecture) The bell or vase of the Corinthian capital.

quote.text: Thus the capital of the Corinthian column always resembles a deep narrow basket covered with a tile, and completely surrounded by foliage

definitions.definition: (informal, euphemistic) Bastard.
(military, aircraft) A drogue (or para-drogue) in the probe-and-drogue refueling method
(transitive) To place in a basket or baskets.
(transitive, publishing) To cross-collateralize the royalty advances for multiple works so that the creator is not paid until all of those works have achieved a certain level of success.
